commons:98691704.summary: At the crown of the dome, Christ stands waist-deep in the Jordan as John the Baptist baptizes him and the dove of the Holy Spirit descends from above; an old river-god personifying the Jordan looks on. Around this golden medallion the twelve apostles process in shimmering robes, carrying crowns. Placed directly over the font, the image showed each newly baptized Christian that they were entering into the baptism of Christ himself.
facts: The dome and its mosaics are credited to Bishop Neon of Ravenna (c. 450–473), who completed the octagonal baptistery begun by his predecessor Ursus beside the city's cathedral.
The central medallion has been heavily restored: the heads of Christ and John, the dove and John's cross are later restorations rather than fifth-century work.
The personified Jordan river-god is a borrowing from classical art, labeled with the river's name.
Because the ground in Ravenna has subsided, the baptistery's original floor now lies some two to three meters below today's street level.

links.label: UNESCO: Early Christian Monuments of Ravenna

commons:98691704.notes: Date: Commons/Wikidata give 5th century; mosaics added under Bishop Neon (bishop c. 450–473). Not already in c-2…c-11 (no Neon Baptistery entry found). Sources differ on whether the heads were remade in the 18th or 19th century; the fact is phrased after Italian Wikipedia.

cur:manuscripts-de-laudibus-amiens-chris.summary: In this copy from the abbey of Corbie, Christ again stands with arms outstretched across a framed grid of letters, his cross-nimbus inscribed and his long hair and beard drawn in dark ink; the outlines of his body enclose separate verses within the poem. The red loincloth and simple flesh tones make the figure stand out from the even field of capitals.
facts: Rabanus Maurus, abbot of Fulda and later Archbishop of Mainz, composed this cycle of figure-poems (carmina figurata) in praise of the Cross around 810; each page is a grid of letters in which shapes pick out further verses.
This manuscript came from the abbey of Corbie and is now in the municipal library of Amiens; it was digitised for the Europeana Regia project.
cur:manuscripts-de-laudibus-amiens-chris.notes: The number in the Commons file name is the Gallica view number, not the folio.

cur:manuscripts-valcavado-he-cometh-with.summary: Christ, haloed and robed, stands with outstretched arms within a great swirling blue mass of cloud, flanked by angels, while below crowds of people — those who 'pierced him' and all the tribes of the earth — gesture and mourn on either side of a mound. Latin captions explain the vision.
facts: The Valcavado Beatus was written and illuminated in 970 by the monk Oveco for Abbot Sempronius of Valcavado, in the reign of Ramiro III of León; it has 230 surviving leaves and 87 miniatures.
After the expulsion of the Jesuits under Charles III, the manuscript passed from their college of San Ambrosio in Valladolid to the University of Valladolid.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-68-christ.summary: Below, the psalmist clings to the stern of a ship as his enemies close in, 'save me, O God, for the waters are come in unto my soul', and men fall away from a table into the sea. In the heavens at the left the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos with two angels orders two wingless angels to blot the names of the unjust out of the book of the living. This is the psalm of 'in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink', quoted in the Passion narratives.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-68-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-85-christ.summary: High in the drawing the psalmist as king points to a poor man with stick and wallet and appeals to the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, who holds a cross-staff and 'bows down his ear': 'Bow down thine ear, O Lord, hear me: for I am poor and needy'. Below, two idols stand on a tall pedestal, 'among the gods there is none like unto thee', and armed men threaten. The drawing illustrates a psalm of humble prayer.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
The psalter was made in or near Reims, probably under Archbishop Ebbo (816–835); some scholars argue for a date around 850 under his successor Hincmar.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-85-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-stuttgart-psalter-psalm.summary: Between bands of coloured sky and sea, a haloed Christ holding a cross-staff stands over a lion and a dragon-like beast, his mantle billowing. The miniature accompanies the verse 'that thy foot may be dipped in the blood of thine enemies, and the tongue of thy dogs in the same', which the artist turned into an image of Christ triumphant over evil.
facts: The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
cur:manuscripts2-stuttgart-psalter-psalm.notes: The image is the full page; the miniature occupies only part of it.

Q116273823.summary: Cut into a small faceted piece of rock crystal, Christ hangs on a cross with a footrest, arms spread wide, flanked by the Virgin and Saint John, with a star and a crescent above the arms of the cross and Greek letters running down either side. Cut as an intaglio seal, it would have left a raised impression of the Crucifixion, a sign of its owner's faith. Its clarity and tiny scale make it an intimate Byzantine devotional object.
facts: The Met dates the seal broadly to the 9th–11th century and records it as rock crystal, about 2 cm high (accession 86.11.38, purchased 1886).
Q116273823.notes: The Greek letters were not read or verified.

vam:O352751.summary: Woven in red, cream, blue and green silk, this small, worn roundel shows a frontal figure with long hair and a halo, both arms raised in the ancient gesture of prayer, standing between two stylised trees. A border of floral motifs and small crosses runs round the edge. The V&A identifies the figure as Christ; it is a rare and delicate witness to Christian imagery on luxury silks of late-antique Egypt.
facts: Samite, a twill-woven silk, is thought to have originated in Sasanian Persia; Byzantine workshops adopted the technique, and it became one of the great luxury textiles of the period (V&A).
The roundel was given to the V&A by Robert Taylor in 1900; the museum dates it to about AD 500–700 and attributes it to Egypt.
vam:O352751.notes: The identification as Christ follows the V&A. The orans (praying) pose is more usual for saints, the Virgin or the deceased than for Christ, and no inscription or cross-nimbus confirms the identity, so it should be treated as uncertain.
